newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore seeks improved relations with Malaysia.
newsitem.headline: Singapore seeks improved relations with Malaysia.

text.p: Singapore and Malaysia need to move relations to a higher level of cooperation based on mutual respect and benefit to overcome current strains, Singapore leaders said on Thursday.

"If Singapore and Malaysia can embark on a new era of cooperation, we will signal to the present and future generations that we have discarded the old historical and emotional baggage in favour of fruitful, mutually beneficial cooperation," Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong told parliament.
Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar said Singapore was committed to establishing a long-term relationship with Malaysia provided it was a "cooperation as equals".

Singapore was separated from Malaysia after a brief and bitter marriage between 1963 and 1965. Relations hit a new low after former Singapore prime minister Lee Kuan Yew was deemed to have insulted Malaysia in March.

Lee called Malaysia's southern state of Johore "notorious for shootings, muggings and carjackings," triggering a furious row that ended at government level after two apologies and a withdrawal of an affidavit in which he made the comment.
Newspapers in the two countries have continued sniping at each other, however, and Singapore members of parliament leapt into the still simmering row this week.
They urged the government to accelerate efforts to reduce Singapore's heavy dependence on Malaysian water and not to be held ransom by Malaysian threats to cut supplies.
On Thursday, Goh made public a proposal he made to Malaysian counterpart Mahathir Mohammad last year to secure Singapore's water supplies.

Goh said Singapore was prepared to meet Malaysian demands over land its railway owns in Singapore provided Kuala Lumpur agreed to extend a water supply pact indefinitely after 2061 when the current deal expires.

Lee and then Malaysian finance minister Daim Zainuddin signed a deal in November 1990 under which Malaysian Railways would move its station from valuable land in near Singapore's business district to the less populated north.
In return, the two countries would form a company to develop the vacated land and two other Malaysian railway-owned plots. Malaysia would own 60 percent of the company and Singapore the rest.
But after the deal was sealed, Mahathir wanted changes in the complex details.
Goh, who succeeded Lee, said it would be hard for him to agree to Mahathir's demands unless there was a Malaysian response on water.
Otherwise, it would "undermine the sanctity of all agreements and treaties Singapore has concluded in the past or will sign in the future", Goh told parliament.
